mainTopic: End of ניחוש; the משניות on מחלל שבת and on cursing a parent, and the sources for the punishment and the warning against cursing a parent
overview: This amud finishes the examples of ניחוש, treating ordinary events or animals as signs of luck. A new משנה then teaches that one who desecrates Shabbos is stoned, but only for an act that brings כרת if done on purpose and a חטאת if done by accident. The גמרא infers that some desecration of Shabbos has neither punishment, such as תחומין according to רבי עקיבא or הבערה according to רבי יוסי. The next משנה teaches that one who curses a parent is stoned only if he uses the שם, and the גמרא identifies the חכמים who exempt a כינוי as רבי מנחם ברבי יוסי. A ברייתא then works through the פסוק about cursing a parent: who is included, whether one parent alone is enough (רבי יאשיה and רבי יונתן), and that the death is סקילה. Next it searches for the אזהרה. It tries a הצד השוה from the דיין, the נשיא and the חרש, but rejects it and learns the warning from the extra word אֱלֹהִים instead. Finally the גמרא shows how this works even for the view that אֱלֹהִים means ה׳, pointing to the Torah's choice of the word תְקַלֵּל.

steps.title: Last examples of a person who reads bad omens
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא finishes its list of things a מנחש says: 'Don't start with me,' 'It's morning,' 'It's ראש חודש,' 'It's מוצאי שבת.'
steps.simpleTranslation: A מנחש is also someone who says: 'Don't start with me,' 'It's morning,' 'It's ראש חודש,' 'It's מוצאי שבת.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is finishing a list from the previous lines. The list gives examples of a מנחש, someone who treats normal events as signs of luck.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each line is a person refusing to lose money at a 'beginning': being the first one asked, the start of the day, the start of the month, or the start of the week. He fears a bad start means bad luck for the whole stretch of time. Superstitious thinking like this is what the Torah calls ניחוש.

keyTerms.meaning: Someone who reads signs or omens to predict good or bad luck
Morning, the start of the day
The first day of a new month
The night after Shabbos ends, the start of the new week

phrases.english: "Do not start with me,"
phrases.notes: This is still the list of things a מנחש says. Here he refuses to be the first person someone collects money from, because he sees that as a bad sign.

phrases.english: "It is morning,"
"It is the New Month,"
"It is the end of Shabbos."

steps.triggerLanguage: ״אַל תַּתְחִיל בִּי״, ״שַׁחֲרִית הוּא״
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues a ברייתא from before this section that lists examples of a מנחש.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Avoiding a loss at the 'start' of something (being first, morning, the new month, the new week) out of fear of bad luck counts as ניחוש.

steps.title: Reading signs from a weasel, birds, or fish
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא teaches that the פסוק 'לא תנחשו ולא תעוננו' covers people who read omens from a weasel, birds, or fish.
steps.simpleTranslation: The רבנן taught: 'Do not practice ניחוש or עונן.' This covers, for example, people who read signs from a weasel, from birds, and from fish.
steps.whatsHappening: A new ברייתא gives more examples of the forbidden practice. This time the signs come from animals.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first list was about things people say about times and situations. This ברייתא adds animals: treating how a weasel, a bird, or a fish behaves as a message about the future. The word כגון ('for example') tells us these are samples, not a complete list.

keyTerms.meaning: The Rabbis taught; introduces a ברייתא
Do not practice divination (reading omens)
And do not practice soothsaying (reading lucky or unlucky times)
For example
A weasel

phrases.english: The Rabbis taught:
"You shall not practice divination nor soothsaying":
phrases.notes: ויקרא 19:26

phrases.english: for example, those who divine
by a weasel, by birds, and by fish.

steps.whatToRemember: ניחוש means treating ordinary events as signs of luck. That includes words and times ('don't start with me,' 'it's ראש חודש') and the behavior of animals (weasels, birds, fish).
steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן: ״לֹא תְנַחֲשׁוּ וְלֹא תְעוֹנֵנוּ״
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a second ברייתא with more examples of the same forbidden practice, closing the topic of ניחוש.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The פסוק forbidding ניחוש includes reading signs from a weasel, birds, or fish.

steps.title: New משנה: stoning for desecrating Shabbos
steps.stepSummary: The משנה teaches that a person who desecrates Shabbos is stoned, but only for an act whose deliberate violation brings כרת and whose accidental violation requires a קרבן חטאת.
steps.simpleTranslation: משנה: One who desecrates Shabbos with an act for which a person gets כרת if he does it on purpose, and brings a חטאת if he does it by accident.
steps.whatsHappening: A new משנה begins. It continues the list of people who are stoned and now adds the one who desecrates Shabbos.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה does not just say 'one who desecrates Shabbos.' It limits the case to acts that carry כרת when done on purpose and a חטאת when done by accident. This narrow wording becomes the topic of the גמרא in the next step.

keyTerms.meaning: Short for מתניתין, 'our משנה'
One who desecrates Shabbos
Doing it on purpose
Doing it by accident, without realizing
Spiritual 'cutting off,' a heavenly punishment
A sin-offering brought for an accidental sin

phrases.english: MISHNAH: One who desecrates Shabbos
with a matter for whose intentional doing one is liable to כרת,
and for its unintentional doing, a sin-offering.

steps.confusionAlert: The stoning is for someone who breaks Shabbos on purpose, with witnesses and a warning. The phrases about כרת and חטאת only describe which kind of act is meant. They do not mean an accidental violator is stoned.
steps.triggerLanguage: מַתְנִי׳ הַמְחַלֵּל אֶת הַשַּׁבָּת בְּדָבָר שֶׁחַיָּיבִין עַל זְדוֹנוֹ כָּרֵת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic: a new משנה on desecrating Shabbos.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Stoning for desecrating Shabbos applies only to acts that carry כרת when done on purpose and a חטאת when done by accident.

steps.title: Inference: some desecration of Shabbos has no כרת or חטאת
steps.stepSummary: From the משנה's careful wording, the גמרא infers that some act counts as חילול שבת but brings neither a חטאת for doing it by accident nor כרת for doing it on purpose.
steps.simpleTranslation: גמרא: This implies there is something that counts as desecrating Shabbos, yet one is not liable to a חטאת for doing it by accident or to כרת for doing it on purpose.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא reads the משנה's extra words closely and draws a conclusion from them. This sets up the next move, where the גמרא will try to figure out which act the משנה means to exclude.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If every Shabbos violation carried כרת and a חטאת, the משנה would not need to add that condition. So the extra wording must be there to exclude some real Shabbos prohibition that lacks those punishments. The גמרא has not yet said what that act is.

keyTerms.meaning: Short for גמרא, the discussion of the משנה
By implication; this shows that
That there is something
Desecration of Shabbos

phrases.english: GEMARA: By implication, there is something
that is a desecration of Shabbos,

phrases.aramaic: וְאֵין חַיָּיבִין לֹא עַל שִׁגְגָתוֹ חַטָּאת
phrases.english: and one is not liable to a sin-offering for doing it by accident,
nor to כרת for doing it on purpose.

steps.whyThisMatters: This inference opens the next discussion: which Shabbos prohibition is a real desecration yet falls outside the usual punishments of כרת and חטאת.
steps.triggerLanguage: מִכְּלָל דְּאִיכָּא מִידֵּי דְּחִילּוּל שַׁבָּת הָוֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Analyzes the limiting wording of the משנה in step 3 and draws an inference from it.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Since the משנה specifies acts with כרת and a חטאת, there must be some Shabbos desecration that has neither.

steps.title: Which act is this?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks which Shabbos act counts as חילול שבת but brings neither a חטאת nor כרת.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is it?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks a short question to identify the act it just inferred from the משנה. It is setting up the answer that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 4 showed that some Shabbos act is a desecration but carries no חטאת and no כרת. Now the גמרא wants to know which act that could be.

keyTerms.meaning: What is it? A request to identify something.

phrases.english: What is it?
phrases.notes: He means: which Shabbos act is a desecration but has no חטאת and no כרת, as inferred in the last step.

steps.triggerLanguage: מַאי הִיא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks the גמרא to identify the act implied by the inference in step 4.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Which Shabbos act counts as חילול שבת without bringing a חטאת or כרת.

steps.title: Shabbos boundaries or lighting a fire
steps.stepSummary: The answer is תחומין according to רבי עקיבא, or הבערה according to רבי יוסי.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is the Shabbos boundaries, following רבי עקיבא. Or it is lighting a fire, following רבי יוסי.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives two possible acts. Each one fits the inference according to a particular תנא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי עקיבא holds that walking past the Shabbos boundary is forbidden by the Torah, but it is only a plain prohibition with no כרת and no חטאת. רבי יוסי holds that הבערה is set apart from the other מלאכות and carries only lashes. So according to either view, there is a Shabbos act that is a desecration but does not bring the harsher punishments.

keyTerms.meaning: The Shabbos boundaries, the limit of how far one may walk on Shabbos
Lighting a fire on Shabbos
According to the view of

steps.whatToRemember: The inference from the משנה fits two acts: תחומין according to רבי עקיבא, and הבערה according to רבי יוסי.

phrases.english: Shabbos boundaries, and according to Rabbi Akiva.
phrases.notes: רבי עקיבא holds the boundary rule comes from the Torah, so breaking it really is a desecration of Shabbos.

phrases.english: Kindling a fire, and according to Rabbi Yosei.

steps.triggerLanguage: תְּחוּמִין, וְאַלִּיבָּא דְּרַבִּי עֲקִיבָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 5.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: תחומין according to רבי עקיבא, or הבערה according to רבי יוסי.

steps.title: Cursing a parent requires the שם
steps.stepSummary: The משנה teaches that one who curses a parent is liable only if he uses the שם. If he uses a כינוי, רבי מאיר says he is liable and the חכמים say he is exempt.
steps.simpleTranslation: One who curses his father or mother is not liable unless he curses them using God's name. If he cursed them using a substitute name, רבי מאיר holds him liable and the חכמים exempt him.
steps.whatsHappening: A new משנה begins with a new topic: the death penalty for cursing a parent. It sets a basic condition and then records a מחלוקת.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Everyone agrees that cursing a parent with the actual שם brings stoning. The argument is only about a curse made with a כינוי, a substitute name for God.

keyTerms.meaning: One who curses his father or his mother
With the actual name of God
A substitute name or title for God
Holds liable / exempt

phrases.english: MISHNA: One who curses his father or his mother
is not liable unless he curses them with the name.
phrases.notes: "The name" means God's own name. The curse is said using it.

phrases.english: If he cursed them with a substitute name,
Rabbi Meir holds him liable, and the Rabbis exempt him.

steps.triggerLanguage: הַמְקַלֵּל אָבִיו וְאִמּוֹ אֵינוֹ חַיָּיב עַד שֶׁיְּקַלְּלֵם בַּשֵּׁם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new משנה on a new topic.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Cursing a parent brings stoning only when the שם is used. Whether a כינוי also counts is a מחלוקת between רבי מאיר and the חכמים.

steps.title: Who are the חכמים?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks which specific תנא is meant by the חכמים who exempt one who curses with a כינוי.
steps.simpleTranslation: Who are the חכמים?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens its discussion of the משנה by asking who the unnamed חכמים are. It is setting up the identification that follows.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה gives a group opinion with no name attached. The גמרא wants to trace that opinion to a specific תנא.

keyTerms.meaning: Who?
The Sages, an unnamed group opinion in the משנה

phrases.english: GEMARA: Who are the Rabbis?

steps.triggerLanguage: מַאן חֲכָמִים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks about the unnamed opinion in the משנה of step 7.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The identity of the חכמים who exempt one who curses with a כינוי.

steps.title: It is רבי מנחם ברבי יוסי
steps.stepSummary: The חכמים of the משנה are רבי מנחם ברבי יוסי.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is רבי מנחם the son of רבי יוסי.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא names the תנא behind the view of the חכמים. The proof comes in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This identification connects the anonymous view in the משנה to a named תנא whose reasoning is recorded in a ברייתא.

keyTerms.meaning: A תנא, the son of רבי יוסי

phrases.english: It is Rabbi Menachem, son of Rabbi Yosei.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבִּי מְנַחֵם בְּרַבִּי יוֹסֵי הוּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 8.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The חכמים are רבי מנחם ברבי יוסי.

steps.title: The extra word 'שם' teaches the rule
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא shows that רבי מנחם ברבי יוסי learns from the extra word 'שם' in the פסוק about a blasphemer that one who curses a parent is liable only with the שם.
steps.simpleTranslation: As a ברייתא teaches: רבי מנחם ברבי יוסי says, 'When he blasphemes the name, he shall be put to death.' Why does the פסוק say 'the name'? It teaches about one who curses his father or mother, that he is not liable unless he curses them with the name.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא to prove that the view of the חכמים is the view of רבי מנחם ברבי יוסי.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the פסוק about the blasphemer, the word 'שם' looks extra, since the case is obviously about God's name. רבי מנחם uses that extra word to teach that other curses, like cursing a parent, also need the actual שם. So a כינוי does not make him liable, which is exactly the view of the חכמים.

keyTerms.meaning: As a ברייתא teaches
Why does the פסוק need to say this? (the word seems extra)
It teaches about
When he blasphemes the name

steps.whatToRemember: The חכמים of the משנה are רבי מנחם ברבי יוסי. He learns from the extra word 'שם' that cursing a parent with a כינוי does not bring stoning.

phrases.aramaic: דְּתַנְיָא: רַבִּי מְנַחֵם בְּרַבִּי יוֹסֵי אוֹמֵר,
phrases.english: As it is taught: Rabbi Menachem, son of Rabbi Yosei, says,
"When he blasphemes the name he shall be put to death"
phrases.notes: ויקרא 24:16

phrases.english: Why does the verse state "the name"?
phrases.notes: The פסוק already speaks of God's name earlier, so saying "the name" again looks extra.

phrases.english: It taught about one who curses his father or mother
that he is not liable unless he curses them with the name.

steps.triggerLanguage: דְּתַנְיָא: רַבִּי מְנַחֵם בְּרַבִּי יוֹסֵי אוֹמֵר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports the identification made in step 9 with a ברייתא.
steps.raayaObject: That the חכמים, who exempt one who curses with a כינוי, are רבי מנחם ברבי יוסי.
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא in which רבי מנחם ברבי יוסי learns from the extra word 'שם' (ויקרא 24:16) that cursing a parent requires the שם.

steps.title: 'איש איש' includes a daughter, טומטום, and אנדרוגינוס
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא learns from the doubled word 'איש איש' that the law of cursing a parent also applies to a daughter, a טומטום, and an אנדרוגינוס.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Rabbis taught: 'A man.' Why does the פסוק say 'any man' by repeating the word? To include a daughter, a טומטום, and an אנדרוגינוס.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new ברייתא about who is liable for cursing a parent. It reads the doubled word in the פסוק as including more people.
steps.deeperAnalysis: One 'איש' alone might suggest that only a son is liable. The extra 'איש' widens the law to a daughter, to a טומטום (whose gender cannot be determined), and to an אנדרוגינוס (who has both male and female features).

keyTerms.meaning: The Rabbis taught (introduces a ברייתא)
'Any man', literally 'a man, a man'
To include
A person whose gender cannot be determined
A person with both male and female features

phrases.english: The Rabbis taught: "A man"
phrases.notes: The פסוק is ויקרא 20:9, about one who curses his father or mother.

phrases.english: Why does the verse state "any man"?
To include a daughter, a tumtum, and a hermaphrodite.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן: ״אִישׁ״ – מָה תַּלְמוּד לוֹמַר ״אִישׁ אִישׁ״
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves to a new question about the law of cursing a parent: who is liable.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: From 'איש איש', a daughter, a טומטום, and an אנדרוגינוס are also liable for cursing a parent.

steps.title: What if he curses only one parent?
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא notes that the פסוק mentions both father and mother. It asks for the source that cursing just one of them also makes a person liable.
steps.simpleTranslation: The פסוק says 'who curses his father and his mother.' That only teaches me about both together. Where do I learn the law for cursing his father without his mother, or his mother without his father?
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא raises a question about the wording of the פסוק. It is setting up the next step, where it will bring the answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The words 'his father and his mother' could be read as requiring that he curse both parents. The ברייתא wants a source showing that cursing just one parent is enough.

keyTerms.meaning: I only have (this case): a simple reading teaches only this much
From where do we learn it?
he curses

phrases.english: "That curses his father and his mother"
phrases.notes: ויקרא 20:9

phrases.english: I have only his father and his mother (together).
His father but not his mother,
his mother but not his father, from where do we know?

steps.triggerLanguage: אֵין לִי אֶלָּא אָבִיו וְאִמּוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the same ברייתא, which is going through the פסוק about cursing a parent word by word.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: A source that a person is liable for cursing only one parent.

steps.title: רבי יאשיה: the word order shows each parent counts alone
steps.stepSummary: רבי יאשיה answers from the end of the פסוק, 'אביו ואמו קלל', that cursing either parent alone is enough.
steps.simpleTranslation: The פסוק teaches: 'His father and his mother he has cursed; his blood is upon him.' This means he cursed his father, or he cursed his mother. These are the words of רבי יאשיה.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא answers the question by pointing to how the words are arranged in the פסוק. This answer belongs to רבי יאשיה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: At the start of the פסוק, 'curse' comes right next to 'his father.' At the end, 'cursed' comes right next to 'his mother.' So each parent is tied to the cursing on its own, and cursing either one alone makes him liable.

keyTerms.meaning: The פסוק teaches (introduces the source)
his blood is upon him: a phrase showing he deserves death
תנא who reads 'and' as requiring both unless the פסוק shows otherwise

phrases.english: The verse teaches:
"His father and his mother he has cursed; his blood is upon him"
He cursed his father; he cursed his mother.
phrases.notes: 'Curse' sits next to 'father' at the start of the פסוק and next to 'mother' at the end, so each one counts alone.

phrases.english: These are the words of Rabbi Yoshiya.

steps.triggerLanguage: תַּלְמוּד לוֹמַר: אָבִיו וְאִמּוֹ קִלֵּל דָּמָיו בּוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 12.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The order of words in the פסוק ('יקלל את אביו' at the start, 'אמו קלל' at the end) shows that cursing either parent alone makes him liable.

steps.title: רבי יונתן: 'and' already means together or apart
steps.stepSummary: רבי יונתן holds that 'his father and his mother' already includes each one alone, unless the Torah adds the word 'יחדו' (together).
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יונתן says: The wording means both of them together, and it also means each one by itself, unless the פסוק spells out for you 'together.'
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יונתן gives a different approach. He says there is no need for a special source.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For רבי יונתן, 'X and Y' in the Torah normally covers both together and each one separately. Only when the Torah writes 'יחדו' does it require both together. So the question of step 12 never begins for him.

keyTerms.meaning: it implies / the wording means
by itself, on its own
together
תנא who reads 'and' as including each one separately

steps.whatToRemember: רבי יאשיה needs a special source to include one parent alone. רבי יונתן says 'and' already includes each one alone, unless the Torah writes 'יחדו'.

phrases.english: Rabbi Yonatan says:
It implies both of them together,
and it implies each one by itself,
unless the verse spells out for you "together."

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבִּי יוֹנָתָן אוֹמֵר: מַשְׁמָע שְׁנֵיהֶן כְּאֶחָד
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Disagrees with רבי יאשיה about whether a special source is needed.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The word 'and' covers both together and each one separately, unless the Torah writes 'יחדו'.

steps.title: Is the death penalty stoning or some other death?
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא states that 'מות יומת' here means סקילה. It then asks how we know it is not one of the other deaths in the Torah.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'He shall surely be put to death' means by stoning. Do you say by stoning, or perhaps it is one of all the other deaths stated in the Torah?
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא states that the punishment is סקילה, then questions how we know that. It is setting up the proof in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'מות יומת' by itself does not name which of the four death penalties is meant. So the ברייתא needs a source that points to סקילה in particular.

keyTerms.meaning: he shall surely be put to death
stoning, one of the four court death penalties
the death penalties stated in the Torah

phrases.english: "Shall surely be put to death": by stoning.
You say by stoning,
or is it perhaps only by one
of all the deaths stated in the Torah?

steps.triggerLanguage: אַתָּה אוֹמֵר בִּסְקִילָה, אוֹ אֵינוֹ אֶלָּא בְּאַחַת מִכׇּל מִיתוֹת הָאֲמוּרוֹת בַּתּוֹרָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves on to the next part of the same פסוק, which is the punishment.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: A source that the death penalty for cursing a parent is סקילה.

steps.title: גזירה שווה from 'his blood is upon him'
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא compares 'דמיו בו' here with 'דמיהם בם' by אוב and ידעוני, where the Torah clearly says סקילה.
steps.simpleTranslation: It says here 'his blood is upon him,' and it says elsewhere 'their blood is upon them.' Just as there it is by stoning, so too here it is by stoning.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא proves that the punishment is סקילה by matching a phrase here with the same phrase in another פסוק.
steps.deeperAnalysis: By אוב and ידעוני the Torah writes 'באבן ירגמו אתם, דמיהם בם', so stoning is stated there openly. The shared phrase 'blood upon him/them' carries that punishment over to one who curses a parent.

keyTerms.meaning: It says here... and it says there: the opening of a גזירה שווה
their blood is upon them
just as there... so too here

phrases.english: It is stated here: "His blood is upon him,"
and it is stated elsewhere: "Their blood is upon them."
phrases.notes: ויקרא 20:27, about אוב and ידעוני, where stoning is stated openly.

phrases.english: Just as there it is by stoning,
so too here it is by stoning.

steps.triggerLanguage: נֶאֱמַר כָּאן דָּמָיו בּוֹ, וְנֶאֱמַר לְהַלָּן דְּמֵיהֶם בָּם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 15.
steps.whatToRemember: One who curses a parent gets סקילה. This is learned by a גזירה שווה from 'דמיו בו' / 'דמיהם בם'.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: A גזירה שווה from 'דמיהם בם' by אוב and ידעוני, where the death is stoning.

steps.title: Where is the warning against cursing a parent?
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא has the punishment. Now it asks for the אזהרה, the negative commandment that forbids the act.
steps.simpleTranslation: We have heard the punishment. Where do we get the warning?
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא opens a new question. It is setting up the source that will come in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The Torah normally does not punish without first giving a warning (a לאו). The פסוק of 'מות יומת' gives only the punishment, so a separate source for the prohibition is needed.

keyTerms.meaning: punishment
warning: the prohibition itself
we have heard / learned

steps.confusionAlert: Knowing the punishment is not the same as having the prohibition. The ברייתא wants a separate לאו, even though it already knows the death penalty.

phrases.english: We have heard the punishment;
from where do we get the warning?

steps.triggerLanguage: עוֹנֶשׁ שָׁמַעְנוּ, אַזְהָרָה מִנַּיִין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After setting the punishment, the ברייתא looks for the prohibition.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The source of the negative commandment (אזהרה) against cursing a parent.

steps.title: 'אלהים לא תקלל' covers a father who is a judge or a נשיא
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא brings 'אלהים לא תקלל ונשיא בעמך לא תאר'. A father who is a judge or a נשיא is already covered by these prohibitions.
steps.simpleTranslation: The פסוק teaches: 'You shall not curse judges...' If his father was a judge, he is included in 'You shall not curse judges.' If his father was a נשיא, he is included in 'And a נשיא among your people you shall not curse.'
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא starts answering with the פסוק that forbids cursing judges and a נשיא. It shows that a father who holds one of these roles is already protected.
steps.deeperAnalysis: These prohibitions apply to everyone, so a son who curses a father who is a judge or a נשיא breaks them. At this point the answer only covers a father with a special role. An ordinary father is not yet covered here.

keyTerms.meaning: Do not curse judges (here אלהים means judges)
a judge
a king or leader of the people
do not curse
included in

steps.confusionAlert: This step does not yet give a warning for every father. It only covers a father who is a judge or a נשיא. The ברייתא continues after this to extend the warning to an ordinary father.

phrases.english: The verse teaches: "You shall not curse judges, etc."
phrases.notes: שמות 22:27. Here אלהים means judges, and the 'etc.' stands for 'ונשיא בעמך לא תאר'.

phrases.english: If his father was a judge,
he is included in "You shall not curse judges,"
and if his father was a king,

phrases.aramaic: הֲרֵי הוּא בִּכְלַל ״וְנָשִׂיא בְעַמְּךָ לֹא תָאֹר״.
phrases.english: he is included in "And a king among your people you shall not curse."

steps.triggerLanguage: תַּלְמוּד לוֹמַר: אֱלֹהִים לֹא תְקַלֵּל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Begins answering the question of step 17.
steps.whyThisMatters: This sets the base cases, a father who is a judge and a father who is a נשיא. The ברייתא will build on these to find a warning for every father.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The prohibitions against cursing a judge and a נשיא cover a father who holds one of those roles.

steps.title: What if the father is neither a judge nor a נשיא?
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא asks where we learn the prohibition against cursing a father who holds no special position.
steps.simpleTranslation: If the father is not a judge and not a נשיא, how do we know it is forbidden to curse him?
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא points out a gap in the last answer. Most fathers are not judges or a נשיא, so where is their prohibition?
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 18 only covered a father who happens to be a judge or a נשיא, because the פסוקים speak about those people directly. An ordinary father is not mentioned there. So we still need a source for him.

keyTerms.meaning: A judge
A ruler or leader of the people (the פסוק 'ונשיא בעמך לא תאר')
From where do we know?

phrases.aramaic: אֵינוֹ לֹא דַּיָּין וְלֹא נָשִׂיא, מִנַּיִין?
phrases.english: If he is neither a judge nor a נשיא, from where do we know?
phrases.notes: 'He' is the father. We are still looking for the warning against cursing him.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֵינוֹ לֹא דַּיָּין וְלֹא נָשִׂיא, מִנַּיִין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finds a gap in Step 18's answer, which only covered a father who is a judge or a נשיא.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: A source for the prohibition against cursing an ordinary father who has no special position.

steps.title: Learn it from both cases together
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא suggests building a general rule from both the judge and the נשיא. It first notes that the two are not alike.
steps.simpleTranslation: You can say: learn a general rule from the two of them. The special feature of a נשיא is not like that of a judge, and the special feature of a judge is not like that of a נשיא.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא proposes a method: put the two cases together and learn a general rule from what they share. It is setting up the next move by noting that each case has its own special feature.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A בנין אב משני כתובים works like this. Each case alone has a special feature, so you cannot learn from it alone. But the feature they share can be applied to new cases. Saying 'they are not alike' is the first part of that method.

keyTerms.meaning: A 'model case': a general rule built from a case in the Torah and applied to similar cases
From both of them
'The feature of this one is not like the feature of that one': each case has something unique

steps.confusionAlert: Saying 'they are not alike' does not weaken the proof. It is a normal part of the method. The differences show why we need both cases, and then we use what they have in common.

phrases.english: You can say: you derive it
through a general rule built from both of them.
The feature of a נשיא is not like the feature of a judge,
and the feature of a judge is not like the feature of a נשיא.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמְרַתְּ: הֲרֵי אַתָּה דָּן בִּנְיַן אָב מִשְּׁנֵיהֶן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers Step 19 by proposing a method that combines the two פסוקים from Step 18.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Learn the ordinary father from a general rule built from both the judge and the נשיא.

steps.title: How the judge and the נשיא differ
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא explains each one's special feature. A judge's rulings must be obeyed. Rebelling against a נשיא is forbidden and punished.
steps.simpleTranslation: A judge is not like a נשיא, because with a judge you are commanded to follow his ruling, while with a נשיא you are not commanded to follow his ruling. And a נשיא is not like a judge, because with a נשיא you are commanded about rebelling against him, while with a judge you are not commanded about rebelling against him.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא spells out the difference between the two cases, so we can see why neither one alone can teach the rule for an ordinary father.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A judge has a special feature: we must obey his legal rulings. A נשיא has a different special feature: rebelling against his orders is a crime. Each feature could be the reason for the cursing prohibition, so we cannot learn from just one of them.

keyTerms.meaning: A legal ruling or teaching
Rebelling, disobeying an order
Commanded

phrases.english: The feature of a judge is not like the feature of a נשיא,

phrases.aramaic: שֶׁהֲרֵי דַּיָּין – אַתָּה מְצֻוֶּוה עַל הוֹרָאָתוֹ,
phrases.english: for with a judge, you are commanded about his ruling,

phrases.aramaic: כִּרְאִי נָשִׂיא – שֶׁאִי אַתָּה מְצֻוֶּוה עַל הוֹרָאָתוֹ.
phrases.english: unlike a נשיא, where you are not commanded about his ruling.
And the feature of a נשיא is not like the feature of a judge,
for with a נשיא, you are commanded about rebelling against him,

phrases.aramaic: כִּרְאִי דַּיָּין – שֶׁאִי אַתָּה מְצֻוֶּוה עַל הַמְרָאָתוֹ.
phrases.english: unlike a judge, where you are not commanded about rebelling against him.

steps.triggerLanguage: לֹא רְאִי דַּיָּין כִּרְאִי נָשִׂיא, שֶׁהֲרֵי דַּיָּין אַתָּה מְצֻוֶּוה עַל הוֹרָאָתוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains the two short lines of Step 20 that said the cases are not alike.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A judge's special feature is that his rulings must be obeyed. A נשיא's special feature is that rebelling against him is forbidden.

steps.title: What they share: both are 'of your people'
steps.stepSummary: Both the judge and the נשיא are 'בעמך' and may not be cursed. A father is also 'בעמך', so he may not be cursed either.
steps.simpleTranslation: What they have in common is that they are 'of your people', and you are warned not to curse them. So I will also include your father, who is 'of your people', and you are warned not to curse him.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא finishes the proof. It finds the feature both cases share and applies it to an ordinary father.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Their special features are different, so the cursing ban cannot depend on those. It must depend on what they share: being part of the Jewish people. An ordinary father is also part of the Jewish people, so he is covered by the warning too.

keyTerms.meaning: The common side, the feature both cases share
Among your people, a fellow Jew
Warned, forbidden by a לאו
A curse

phrases.english: The common feature between them
is that they are 'of your people',
phrases.notes: From the פסוק 'ונשיא בעמך לא תאר' (שמות 22:27).

phrases.english: and you are warned against cursing them.
I too will include your father, who is 'of your people',
and you are warned against cursing him.

steps.triggerLanguage: הַצַּד הַשָּׁוֶה שֶׁבָּהֶם שֶׁהֵן בְּעַמְּךָ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the בנין אב by finding the shared feature after Step 21 showed the differences.
steps.raayaObject: The prohibition against cursing an ordinary father.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The common feature of the judge and the נשיא (both 'בעמך') from 'אלהים לא תקלל ונשיא בעמך לא תאר'.

steps.title: But they share something else: high status
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא challenges the proof. The judge and the נשיא also share importance, so maybe that is why they are protected.
steps.simpleTranslation: What about their common feature? They also share that their greatness causes it for them.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא pushes back on its own proof. It points out a second thing the judge and the נשיא share, and an ordinary father does not have it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The proof assumed the only shared feature was 'בעמך'. But both are also important people, and maybe their importance is the reason cursing them is forbidden. If so, an ordinary father, who is not important in that way, would not be included.

keyTerms.meaning: 'What about... since it has...': a standard way to attack a comparison by showing a difference
Greatness, high status

phrases.english: What about the common feature between them?
For their greatness caused it for them!
phrases.notes: He means: maybe they may not be cursed only because they are important people.

steps.triggerLanguage: מָה לְהַצַּד הַשָּׁוֶה שֶׁבָּהֶן, שֶׁכֵּן גְּדוּלָּתָן גָּרְמָה לָהֶן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the בנין אב of Step 22 by naming a second shared feature that a regular father lacks.
steps.kashyaTarget: The בנין אב from judge and נשיא that includes an ordinary father.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Both sources share high status. Maybe that, and not merely being 'בעמך', is the reason for the prohibition, so it cannot be extended to an ordinary father.

steps.title: Bringing a third case: the deaf person
steps.stepSummary: To answer the challenge that judges and the נשיא are protected only because they are important, the ברייתא brings the פסוק 'Do not curse the deaf.' This protects a weak, unimportant person.
steps.simpleTranslation: The verse teaches: 'You shall not curse the deaf.' The verse is talking about the wretched, helpless people among your nation.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא answers the last challenge by adding a new case: the חרש. A deaf person is a weak and helpless person, not an important one.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The challenge in step 23 was that the דיין and the נשיא are both important, so maybe only important people are protected. The חרש shows that even lowly, helpless people are protected from curses. So importance cannot be the only reason for the rule.

keyTerms.meaning: The verse teaches (introduces a פסוק as a source)
A deaf person
Wretched, helpless, unfortunate people
Among your people

phrases.english: The verse teaches:
"You shall not curse the deaf"
phrases.notes: ויקרא 19:14

phrases.english: about the wretched among your people
the verse is speaking.

steps.triggerLanguage: תַּלְמוּד לוֹמַר: לֹא תְקַלֵּל חֵרֵשׁ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge from step 23 by adding a case that has no importance at all.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Adding a third source that does not share the challenged feature (importance)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Maybe only important people like the דיין and the נשיא are protected from curses.
steps.terutzMaskana: The חרש, a helpless person, is also protected, so importance is not the deciding factor.

steps.title: The deaf person has his own special reason
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא challenges the proof from the חרש. Maybe he is protected only because he is deaf and cannot defend himself.
steps.simpleTranslation: But what about a deaf person? His deafness is what caused him to be protected.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא pushes back on the חרש proof. It says the deaf person has his own special reason for being protected.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Maybe the Torah protects the חרש only because his handicap makes cursing him extra cruel, since he cannot hear and respond. If so, you cannot learn from him that an ordinary father is protected, because a father has no such handicap.

keyTerms.meaning: What about...? (a standard opening for pointing out what makes a case special)
Deafness
It caused it for him (it is the reason for his special law)

phrases.english: What about a deaf person?
His deafness caused it for him.
phrases.notes: He means: maybe the deaf man is protected only because of his handicap, a reason a father doesn't have.

steps.triggerLanguage: מָה לְחֵרֵשׁ, שֶׁכֵּן חֲרִישָׁתוֹ גָּרְמָה לוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the new case brought in step 24.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The חרש has a unique feature (his deafness, which makes him helpless) that a father lacks, so you cannot learn from him.

steps.title: The judge and the נשיא prove otherwise
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא answers: the דיין and the נשיא are not deaf, yet they are protected. So deafness cannot be the only reason.
steps.simpleTranslation: The נשיא and the judge will prove it.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא answers the challenge about the חרש by pointing back to the נשיא and the דיין.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If deafness were the only reason for the ban, then healthy, non-deaf people would not be protected. But the נשיא and the דיין are not deaf, and they are protected. So deafness is not what makes the rule.

keyTerms.meaning: They will prove (it is not so)
The leader of the nation
A judge

phrases.english: The נשיא and the judge will prove it.

steps.triggerLanguage: נָשִׂיא וְדַיָּין יוֹכִיחוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge in step 25 by using the earlier cases.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Counter-example: other protected people lack the challenged feature
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Maybe only the deaf are protected, because of their handicap.
steps.terutzMaskana: The נשיא and the דיין are not deaf and are still protected, so deafness is not the deciding factor.

steps.title: But the judge and the נשיא are important
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא repeats the old challenge: the נשיא and the דיין are protected only because of their greatness.
steps.simpleTranslation: But what about the נשיא and the judge? Their greatness is what caused them to be protected.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא raises the same challenge it raised before: the נשיא and the דיין have something special, which is their importance.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is the same point as step 23. If they are protected only because they are great, a plain father cannot be learned from them. The ברייתא is now going back and forth between the cases.

keyTerms.meaning: Greatness, high position

phrases.english: What about the נשיא and the judge?
Their greatness caused it for them.

steps.triggerLanguage: מָה לְנָשִׂיא וְדַיָּין שֶׁכֵּן גְּדוּלָּתָן גָּרְמָה לָהֶן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the answer in step 26 by bringing back the challenge from step 23.
steps.kashyaTarget: The proof from the נשיא and the דיין
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Their importance is a special feature a father lacks, so they cannot teach about a father.

steps.title: The deaf person proves otherwise
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא answers: the חרש is not important, yet he is protected. So greatness cannot be the only reason.
steps.simpleTranslation: The deaf person will prove it.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא answers by pointing again to the חרש, who has no greatness at all and is still protected.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each case answers the challenge against the other. The חרש shows that importance is not needed. The נשיא and the דיין show that a handicap is not needed. This sets up the final move.

keyTerms.meaning: He will prove (it is not so)

phrases.english: The deaf person will prove it.

steps.triggerLanguage: חֵרֵשׁ יוֹכִיחַ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge in step 27 using the case from step 24.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Counter-example: a protected person without the challenged feature
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Maybe only important people are protected.
steps.terutzMaskana: The חרש is protected without being important, so greatness is not the deciding factor.

steps.title: The argument goes in a circle, and the cases are different
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא notes that the argument has come back around. Each case has its own special feature, different from the other.
steps.simpleTranslation: The argument has come back around. This case is not like that one, and that case is not like this one.
steps.whatsHappening: This is a setup line. The ברייתא says the back-and-forth has gone in a circle, and it is getting ready to use the common feature of the cases.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא admits that each case alone has a weakness: the חרש is helpless and the נשיא and דיין are important. But since their special features are different from each other, neither feature can explain the whole rule. This prepares the הצד השוה in the next step.

keyTerms.meaning: The argument has returned (gone around in a circle)
This case's feature is not like that case's feature

steps.confusionAlert: 'וחזר הדין' does not mean the proof failed. It means the cases keep answering each other, so the ברייתא now uses what they share.

phrases.english: And the argument has come back around.
The feature of this one is not like the feature of that one,
phrases.notes: Literally 'the look of this is not like the look of that.' Here it means the נשיא and judge on one side, the deaf man on the other.

phrases.english: and the feature of that one is not like the feature of this one.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְחָזַר הַדִּין. לֹא רְאִי זֶה כִרְאִי זֶה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Sums up the back-and-forth of steps 24 to 28 and sets up the הצד השוה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Each case has a different special feature, so no single special feature explains the ban.

steps.title: The common feature: a father may not be cursed
steps.stepSummary: The common feature of all the cases is that they are 'of your people' and may not be cursed. A father is also 'of your people', so it is forbidden to curse him.
steps.simpleTranslation: What they all share is that they are among your people, and you are warned not to curse them. So I will also include your father, who is among your people, and you are warned not to curse him.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא finishes its proof. It takes the one feature all the cases share and applies it to a father.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The special features (greatness, deafness) cancel each other out, because each case has a different one. What is left is the shared point: they are all Jews, 'of your people.' Since a father also has this feature, the ban on cursing applies to him too.

keyTerms.meaning: The common feature shared by the cases
Warned, forbidden by the Torah
A curse
Your father

steps.whatToRemember: A הצד השוה works when each source alone has a weakness, but the weaknesses are different. Here the shared feature is being 'of your people'. Step 31 attacks this proof, and the final source for a father comes from the extra word אֱלֹהִים in step 32.
steps.whyThisMatters: This shows how a law can be learned from several sources together, even when no single source is strong enough by itself. It also sets up the challenge in the next step, which finds a different feature that all these sources share.

phrases.english: The common feature among them:
that they are among your people,
and you are warned not to curse them.
So I too will include your father,
who is among your people, and you are warned not to curse him.

steps.triggerLanguage: הַצַּד הַשָּׁוֶה שֶׁבָּהֶן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the setup of step 29 by using the shared feature to answer the question from step 19.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: At this stage, the ברייתא proposes a הצד השוה of the דיין, the נשיא and the חרש: an ordinary father is 'of your people', so cursing him is forbidden. Step 31 challenges this proof, and step 32 replaces it.

steps.title: Maybe the shared feature is that they are all unusual
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא attacks the צד השוה. What the חרש, נשיא and דיין have in common may be that each is an unusual person, and a father is not.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is special about what they all share? They are all unusual people.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא attacks the proof from the last step. It points out a different common feature that a father does not have.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A צד השוה only works if the shared feature also fits the new case. Here the challenge says the shared feature might be that each of them is out of the ordinary: the חרש is disabled, and the נשיא and דיין are important. An ordinary father is not unusual, so the proof might not reach him.

keyTerms.meaning: Unusual, different from ordinary people
'In that', which brings in the special feature that blocks a proof

steps.confusionAlert: 'Unusual' here does not mean only 'important'. The חרש is unusual because he is deaf, and the נשיא and דיין are unusual because of their high position. The challenge joins all three under one feature that a regular father lacks.

phrases.english: What is special about their common feature?
That they are unusual!

steps.triggerLanguage: מָה לְצַד הַשָּׁוֶה שֶׁבָּהֶן, שֶׁכֵּן מְשׁוּנִּין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the צד השוה conclusion of step 30
steps.kashyaTarget: The צד השוה proof that a father is included because he is 'of your people'
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: There is a different shared feature, being unusual, that the source cases have and a father lacks. So the proof fails.

steps.title: The extra word אֱלֹהִים teaches about a father
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא gives a new proof. If the rule were only for unusual people, the תורה could have listed just two cases. Listing אֱלֹהִים is extra, so it is used for a father.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather: if so, let the פסוק write either 'judges and deaf' or 'king and deaf'. Why do I need 'judges'? If it is not needed for itself, use it for his father.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא drops the צד השוה and builds a new proof from an extra word in the פסוק.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the rule only covered unusual people, two cases would be enough to teach it: a חרש together with either a דיין or a נשיא. Since the דיין and the נשיא are both important people, one of them is extra. The extra אֱלֹהִים is therefore moved to teach that one may not curse a father.

keyTerms.meaning: If so: if your claim were true
Let the פסוק write; the תורה could have said it more briefly
If it is not needed for its own topic
Apply it to another topic

steps.whatToRemember: An extra word that is not needed for its own topic is moved to teach a new law. Here the extra אֱלֹהִים teaches that cursing a father is forbidden.
steps.whyThisMatters: The proof no longer depends on comparing the cases. It depends on the extra word, so the 'they are unusual' challenge no longer matters.

phrases.english: Rather, if so,
phrases.notes: 'If so' means: if the rule were really only about unusual people.

phrases.english: let the verse write:
either 'judges and deaf,'
or 'king and deaf.'
Why do I need 'judges'?
If it is not needed for its own matter,
apply it to the matter of his father.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא, אִם כֵּן נִכְתּוֹב קְרָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 31 by replacing the צד השוה with a proof from an extra word
steps.terutzResolutionType: New derivation from an extra word in the פסוק
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Maybe the איסור covers only unusual people, so a father would not be included
steps.terutzMaskana: Two cases would have been enough for 'unusual people'. The extra אֱלֹהִים is used to forbid cursing a father.

steps.title: What about the view that אֱלֹהִים means ה׳?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks: the proof works if אֱלֹהִים means judges. But if it means ה׳, the word is not extra, so how do we learn about a father?
steps.simpleTranslation: This works for the one who says 'אֱלֹהִים' is not holy. But for the one who says it is holy, what can be said?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא questions the new proof. It works for only one opinion about what the word אֱלֹהִים means.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The proof needed אֱלֹהִים to be extra, which is true only if it means judges ('חול'). If אֱלֹהִים means ה׳‎ ('קודש'), the word teaches its own law against cursing ה׳. Then nothing is extra to teach about a father.

keyTerms.meaning: This works well, but only according to one view
Not holy: here, the word means human judges
Holy: here, the word means ה׳
What is there to say?

phrases.english: This works well according to the one who says
'elohim' is non-sacred,
phrases.notes: The word אֱלֹהִים is from the פסוק in שמות 22:27. 'Non-sacred' means it refers to judges, not ה׳.

phrases.english: but according to the one who says it is sacred,
what is there to say?

steps.triggerLanguage: הָנִיחָא לְמַאן דְּאָמַר ״אֱלֹהִים״ חוֹל, אֶלָּא לְמַאן דְּאָמַר קוֹדֶשׁ, מַאי אִיכָּא לְמֵימַר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the extra-word proof of step 32
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that אֱלֹהִים is extra and can be moved to teach about a father
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If אֱלֹהִים means ה׳, it is needed for the איסור of cursing ה׳, so it is not extra.

steps.title: Source for the מחלוקת: רבי ישמעאל and רבי עקיבא
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא shows that both views exist. רבי ישמעאל says אֱלֹהִים here means judges. רבי עקיבא says it means ה׳.
steps.simpleTranslation: As it is taught: 'אֱלֹהִים' is not holy, these are the words of רבי ישמעאל. רבי עקיבא says: 'אֱלֹהִים' is holy.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא backs up its question. It quotes a ברייתא showing that there really is an opinion that אֱלֹהִים means ה׳.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This shows the question is not just a guess. רבי עקיבא really holds the 'קודש' view. For him the extra-word proof seems to fail.

keyTerms.meaning: As it is taught in a ברייתא
The words (opinion) of

phrases.english: As it is taught: 'elohim' is non-sacred,
these are the words of Rabbi Yishmael.
Rabbi Akiva says: 'Elohim' is sacred.

steps.triggerLanguage: דְּתַנְיָא: ״אֱלֹהִים״ – חוֹל, דִּבְרֵי רַבִּי יִשְׁמָעֵאל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Shows the source for the 'קודש' opinion mentioned in step 33
steps.raayaObject: That there is a view that אֱלֹהִים in the פסוק means ה׳
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא recording the מחלוקת of רבי ישמעאל and רבי עקיבא

steps.title: רבי אליעזר בן יעקב uses the פסוק for cursing ה׳
steps.stepSummary: A second ברייתא shows the 'holy' reading in use. רבי אליעזר בן יעקב learns the warning against cursing ה׳ from 'אֱלֹהִים לֹא תְקַלֵּל'.
steps.simpleTranslation: And it is taught: רבי אליעזר בן יעקב says: From where is the warning against one who 'blesses' the Name? The פסוק says: 'Do not curse אֱלֹהִים.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings another ברייתא showing that this פסוק is used for the איסור of cursing ה׳. This makes the question stronger.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here the word is clearly being used up for its own law, the warning against cursing ה׳. So on this view it is hard to call אֱלֹהִים extra and move it to a father. The next step answers this question.

keyTerms.meaning: A warning: the תורה's source that something is forbidden
A polite way to say cursing ה׳
The פסוק teaches

steps.confusionAlert: 'מברך' here does not mean blessing. The גמרא says 'bless' to avoid writing the words 'curse ה׳'.

phrases.aramaic: וְתַנְיָא: רַבִּי אֱלִיעֶזֶר בֶּן יַעֲקֹב אוֹמֵר:
phrases.english: And it is taught: Rabbi Eliezer ben Ya'akov says:
From where is the warning against one who 'blesses' the Name?
phrases.notes: 'Blesses' is a polite way of saying 'curses'. No one wants to write 'curse ה׳' outright.

phrases.english: The verse says: 'You shall not curse Elohim.'
phrases.notes: שמות 22:27

steps.triggerLanguage: וְתַנְיָא: רַבִּי אֱלִיעֶזֶר בֶּן יַעֲקֹב אוֹמֵר: אַזְהָרָה לִמְבָרֵךְ אֶת הַשֵּׁם מִנַּיִין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a second source showing the פסוק used for cursing ה׳
steps.raayaObject: That 'אֱלֹהִים לֹא תְקַלֵּל' is used for the איסור of cursing ה׳
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא of רבי אליעזר בן יעקב

steps.title: Both views learn both prohibitions
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers the question from step 33. Each view learns the second prohibition from the first. One view learns holy (ה׳) from non-holy (judges). The other learns non-holy from holy.
steps.simpleTranslation: According to the one who says 'אֱלֹהִים' means judges, he learns the rule for ה׳ from the rule for judges. According to the one who says 'אֱלֹהִים' means ה׳, we learn the rule for judges from the rule for ה׳.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers its own question. No matter which meaning of אֱלֹהִים you take, the פסוק ends up forbidding cursing both judges and ה׳.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In step 33 the worry was this: if אֱלֹהִים means ה׳, then the word is not extra, and we cannot use it for a father. The answer is that each view reads the פסוק as covering both cases. The difference is only which case is written directly and which one is learned from it.

keyTerms.meaning: Non-holy. Here it means the reading where אֱלֹהִים refers to human judges.
Holy. Here it means the reading where אֱלֹהִים refers to ה׳.
He learns (one law from another).
According to the one who says.

phrases.english: According to the one who says "אֱלֹהִים" is non-holy,
phrases.notes: Here 'non-holy' means human judges, and 'holy' means ה׳.

phrases.english: he learns the holy from the non-holy.
According to the one who says "אֱלֹהִים" is holy,
we learn the non-holy from the holy.

steps.triggerLanguage: לְמַאן דְּאָמַר ״אֱלֹהִים״ חוֹל – גָּמַר קוֹדֶשׁ מֵחוֹל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question raised in step 33, using the two views shown in steps 34 and 35.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Shows that both readings produce both prohibitions, each through a different direction of learning.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: If אֱלֹהִים means ה׳, it covers only ה׳, so nothing in the word is left over for a father.
steps.terutzMaskana: Both views learn both prohibitions, so the overall structure of the derivation holds for each view.

steps.title: Can the holy reading really teach about judges?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא accepts that the judges-view can learn ה׳ from judges. It questions whether the ה׳-view can learn judges from ה׳. Maybe the Torah warns only about ה׳.
steps.simpleTranslation: Granted, according to the one who says 'אֱלֹהִים' means judges, he can learn the rule for ה׳ from the rule for judges. But according to the one who says 'אֱלֹהִים' means ה׳, can he learn the rule for judges from the rule for ה׳? Maybe the Torah warned only about ה׳ and not about judges!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on half of the answer it just gave. Learning from judges to ה׳ makes sense, but learning from ה׳ down to judges does not seem to follow.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If cursing a judge is forbidden, then cursing ה׳ is surely forbidden, so that direction works. The other direction is weak. A ban on cursing ה׳ does not show that cursing an ordinary judge is also banned.

keyTerms.meaning: Granted; this part makes sense.
Perhaps; maybe.
He (the Torah) warned; gave a prohibition.

phrases.english: Granted, according to the one who says "אֱלֹהִים" is non-holy,
he learns the holy from the non-holy.
phrases.notes: He means: if cursing a judge is forbidden, cursing ה׳ surely is.

phrases.english: But according to the one who says "אֱלֹהִים" is holy,
does he learn the non-holy from the holy?
Maybe the Torah warned about the holy,
and did not warn about the non-holy?

steps.triggerLanguage: בִּשְׁלָמָא לְמַאן דְּאָמַר ״אֱלֹהִים״ חוֹל, גָּמַר קוֹדֶשׁ מֵחוֹל. אֶלָּא לְמַאן דְּאָמַר ״אֱלֹהִים״ קוֹדֶשׁ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the second half of the answer given in step 36.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that the view reading אֱלֹהִים as ה׳ can learn the prohibition on cursing judges from it.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Learning from the more serious case (ה׳) does not prove the less serious case (judges). The Torah may have warned only about ה׳.

steps.title: The wording 'תְקַלֵּל' shows that judges are included
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers from the Torah's wording. If only ה׳ were meant, the פסוק could have said the shorter 'לֹא תָקֵל'. Writing 'תְקַלֵּל' shows that judges are included too.
steps.simpleTranslation: If so, that only ה׳ is meant, let the פסוק write: 'You shall not treat lightly' (לֹא תָקֵל)!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא defends the ה׳-view. It points to the exact word the Torah chose.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the פסוק were only about ה׳, the shorter word 'תָקֵל' would have been enough. Instead the Torah wrote 'תְקַלֵּל'. That different wording is what lets the ה׳-view also include judges.

keyTerms.meaning: If so; if what you said were true.
Let the פסוק write; the Torah should have written.
Treat lightly; disrespect (the shorter word the Torah did not use).
Curse (the word the Torah actually used).

steps.whatToRemember: Both views forbid cursing both ה׳ and judges. The judges-view learns ה׳ from judges, which is the easy direction. The ה׳-view includes judges because the Torah wrote 'תְקַלֵּל' instead of the shorter 'תָקֵל'.

phrases.english: If so,
let the verse write: "You shall not treat lightly"!
phrases.notes: The פסוק actually says 'לֹא תְקַלֵּל' (שמות 22:27). The shorter word would have been enough for ה׳ alone.

steps.triggerLanguage: אִם כֵּן, לִכְתּוֹב קְרָא: ״לֹא תָקֵל״
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 37.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Proof from the Torah's choice of words.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ה׳-view has no source for a prohibition on cursing judges.
steps.terutzMaskana: The longer word 'תְקַלֵּל', used instead of 'תָקֵל', shows that judges are included even for the ה׳-view.
